content: The implementation and impact of the guidelines will be evaluated and monitored through the annual WHO Global Tuberculosis (TB) Surveillance and Monitoring System. This will also involve technical assistance missions and reviews of National TB Programs. The WHO Global Tuberculosis Programme (WHO/GTB) will reassess and update these policy recommendations within four to five years of their release, or sooner if new evidence emerges. The WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (2nd edition, 2014) provides a framework for creating evidence-based guidelines. The GRADE approach, as outlined by Schünemann et al. (2013), is used to assess the quality of evidence and the strength of recommendations. The WHO's 2016 update on treatment guidelines for drug-resistant tuberculosis emphasizes the importance of detecting mutations in katG and inhA genes to guide the use of isoniazid and ethionamide in drug-resistant TB cases. Studies, such as those by Gegia et al. (2017) and Jawahar et al. (2013), have systematically reviewed and analyzed the treatment of isoniazid-resistant TB using first-line drugs, including moxifloxacin and gatifloxacin-containing regimens. Clinical trials, such as those by Merle et al. (2014) and Gillespie et al. (2014), have explored four-month regimens containing gatifloxacin or moxifloxacin for treating drug-sensitive TB. These studies highlight the potential for shorter treatment durations while maintaining efficacy. Fox et al. (2016) utilized propensity score-based approaches to address confounding factors in individual patient data meta-analyses for multidrug-resistant TB treatment. The Cochrane Collaboration (2011) and Tugwell et al. (2010) have emphasized the advantages of individual patient data analyses in systematic reviews. Population-based studies, such as those by Zignol et al. (2016), have investigated resistance patterns of Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates to pyrazinamide and fluoroquinolones. These findings are critical for guiding treatment strategies. Pharmacokinetic studies, such as those by Ramachandran et al. (2012) and Fish et al. (1997), have examined the effects of rifampicin and isoniazid on the steady-state pharmacokinetics of moxifloxacin and levofloxacin, respectively. These studies provide insights into drug interactions and optimization of TB treatment regimens. The WHO's consolidated guidelines on antiretroviral drug use (2016) and systematic reviews, such as those by Ahmad Khan et al. (2012), have addressed the treatment of active TB in patients with HIV infection. These guidelines emphasize a public health approach to managing co-infections. Adverse events associated with TB treatment, including hepatotoxicity and ototoxicity, have been documented in studies by Andrade et al. (2011) and Voogt et al. (1996). These findings underscore the need for careful monitoring during therapy. The WHO's guideline development process involves a structured agenda, including presentations on global surveillance data, systematic reviews, and discussions on treatment regimens for isoniazid-resistant TB. Key issues, such as pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics and resistance detection, are addressed to inform guideline recommendations. The PICO question guiding the guideline development focuses on identifying the optimal treatment regimen composition and duration for isoniazid-resistant TB (excluding MDR-TB) that maximizes treatment success while minimizing harm.
